{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. It is multi-paradigm, drawing on functional ideas such as immutability, higher-order functions, and pattern matching [1].

## Origins

Graydon Hoare began Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. It was first released publicly in 2010, with version 1.0 arriving in 2015 [2]. Its syntax is similar to C++, but it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

## What Memory Safety Means

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, so they are memory-unsafe [3].

## Rust's Approach

Rust shifts these checks to compile time instead of relying on garbage collection. Ownership, borrowing, and lifetime rules let the compiler verify memory access before a program runs.

## Conclusion

{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose language that balances performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Its multi-paradigm design draws on functional ideas such as immutability and pattern matching [1].

## Origins

Graydon Hoare began Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. It was first released publicly in 2010, with version 1.0 arriving in 2015 [2]. Its syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

## What Memory Safety Means

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java enforces it through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, making them memory-unsafe [3].

## Rust's Approach

Rust moves these checks to compile time rather than relying on garbage collection. Ownership, borrowing, and lifetime rules let the compiler verify memory access before a program runs.

## Conclusion

Rust thus delivers memory safety without a garbage collector, though developers must learn its stricter rules.

{"text":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose language that balances performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Its multi-paradigm design draws on functional ideas such as immutability and pattern matching [1].

## Origins

Graydon Hoare began Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. It was first released publicly in 2010, with version 1.0 arriving in 2015 [2]. Its syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

## What Memory Safety Means

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java enforces it through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, making them memory-unsafe [3].

## Rust's Approach

Rust moves these checks to compile time rather than relying on garbage collection. Ownership, borrowing, and lifetime rules let the compiler verify memory access before a program runs.

## Conclusion

Rust thus delivers memory safety without a garbage collector, though developers must learn its stricter rules.","sources":"[1] Wikipedia: Rust (programming language)

Rust is syntactically similar to C++ but guarantees memory safety without needing a garbage collector.

URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_safety
Summary: Memory safety is the state of being protected from various software bugs and security vulnerabilities when dealing with memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers. For example, Java is memory-safe because its runtime error detection checks array bounds and pointer dereferences. By contrast, programming languages like C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic with pointers implemented as direct memory addresses with no provision for bounds checking, making them memory-unsafe.
